newsitem.title: USA: Johnson Controls reaches tentative pact with UAW.
newsitem.headline: Johnson Controls reaches tentative pact with UAW.

text.p: Johnson Controls Inc. said Thursday it reached tentative three-year contract agreements with the United Auto Workers union, ending a 24-day strike that disrupted production of one of Ford Motor Co. most profitable vehicles.

The contracts cover about 500 workers at a seat assembly plant in Plymouth, Mich., and another in Oberlin, Ohio. UAW officials said workers will receive pay increases ranging from 22 percent to 50 percent over the next 24 months. New workers had starting hourly base wages of $9, the union has said.

UAW President Stephen Yokich and UAW Region 1A Director Bob King said the pacts give workers their first ever defined benefit pension plan, comprehensive health care and fully paid holidays equivalent to those of Big Three auto workers.
Johnson Controls officials portrayed the agreements as "fair and reasonable" in terms of its business goals.

"The wage and benefit packages that have been tentatively accepted by the UAW are very much within the range of what we expected for the labour markets in the Plymouth and Oberlin areas," said Chip McClure, general manager for Johnson Controls, in a statement.

Other details of the agreements were not released. The union had been pressing for the company to pledge neutrality in organising attempts at other plants. Only six of Johnson Controls' 34 U.S. facilities are unionized.

A source close to the situation said the contracts do not include any neutrality language. However, union sources said the deals do have some provisions that relate to future union organising efforts.

Ratification meetings are scheduled for Friday morning. Workers at the plants agreed to be represented by the UAW last summer. The deals are the first contracts between the two plants and workers. Johnson Controls said it expects to resume production this coming weekend.

The Plymouth plant has about 300 hourly workers and makes seats for the Expedition full-size sport utility vehicle. The Oberlin plant employs about 200 hourly workers and makes seats for the Econoline and Club Wagon full-size vans.
The tentative contracts close for now an unprecedented chapter in relations between automakers, suppliers and organised labour.

Taking a cue from Ford, Johnson Controls did not fight the UAW's attempts to organise the plant. But talks on a contract broke down as the UAW pushed for base pay levels equal to the $14 to $16 an hour that competitor Lear Corp. pays.

In a highly unusual move, Ford refused to accept seats made by non-union replacements. It continued to build seatless vehicles, believing the strike would be over soon, but eventually shut the lines down.

Ford changed directions again Feb. 12 when it restarted Expedition production with rear seats from Lear and front seats from Ford's own Chesterfield, Mich., trim plant. As of Thursday, the company had shipped 1,700 Expeditions to dealers since production was resumed.

Ford spokesman Bert Serre said Thursday that Lear and the Chesterfield facility will continue to assemble seats for the 12,700 Expeditions that have been produced without seats. Once those vehicles are retrofitted, only Johnson Controls will be the Expedition seat supplier, he said.
Ford has not yet decided when it will resume production at its Econoline assembly line in Lorain, Ohio, and a related frame and paint operation in Avon Lake, Ohio.

Ford's decision to support the union will reverberate in the mostly non-union independent supplier industry, which is under intense pressure from automakers to cut costs, said Donna Parolini, president of International Business Development Corp, a Troy, Mich.-based consultant.
Suppliers now question whether Ford truly wants a partner relationship, a sentiment that could lead to them not bidding on future work, she said.
"Behavior speaks louder than words, and Ford's action said something different than what they've been saying all along," she said.
Johnson Controls stock gained 62.5 cents to $86 on the New York Stock Exchange. Ford edged up 25 cents to $33, also on the NYSE.
